content:
Many Christians picture prayer as standing, sitting or kneeling, and think of the forehead on the ground as a "Muslim" posture, foreign to the worship Jesus (peace be upon him) knew. The Gospels record otherwise. On the night of his arrest, Matthew says, he "fell on his face, and prayed" (Matthew 26:39).[1]

A second question follows from the first. If Jesus lay face down before God and asked that God's will be done over his own, what does the posture say about who he was?

This article aims to provide context to that question, insha'Allah, in five passages: the Gospel scene itself, three from the Hebrew Bible, and the place full prostration still holds in Christian worship. The Quran's own words frame the answer: "O ye who believe! bow down, prostrate yourselves, and adore your Lord" (22:77).[2]

Matthew 26:39 reads: "He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.'" Mark 14:35 says he "fell on the ground", and Luke 22:41 that he "knelt down". The three accounts describe one night, and all three put his body low.[1]

Angela Kim Harkins of Boston College reads the scene against the prayers of Ezra 9, Daniel 9 and the Qumran hymns, where supplication, confession and mourning were joined in one bodily rite. On her reading, the Gethsemane prayer belongs to a recognisable Jewish practice of urgent petition.[3]

The words are as plain as the posture. The one praying asks, and then yields his will to another. Hebrews 5:7 remembers the same night as "prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death".[4]

Genesis 17:3 opens the covenant of circumcision with the same gesture: "Abram fell on his face. God talked with him." The friend of God receives the covenant lying on the ground.[5]

The Quran gives Abraham the same response in words. "Behold! his Lord said to him: 'Bow (thy will to Me):' He said: 'I bow (my will) to the Lord and Cherisher of the Universe'" (2:131).[2]

Genesis does not describe the full sequence of the Muslim prayer, and we claim no more for it than the text says. It shows that a prophet of God answered God by putting his face to the ground, centuries before Sinai.

When the people of Israel turned on them at Meribah, "Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the assembly to the door of the Tent of Meeting, and fell on their faces" (Numbers 20:6). In Numbers 16:22 they do the same in the rebellion of Korah, and plead: "God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?"[5]

Here prostration is the posture of dependence in a crisis, outside any fixed hour of prayer. Islam keeps the same two settings: the five set prayers, and the prostration of a believer who turns to God when trouble comes.

Psalm 95:6 makes the posture an invitation to the whole people: "Oh come, let's worship and bow down. Let's kneel before Yahweh, our Maker, for he is our God."[5]

The Hebrew and Greek words for bowing could also be used of homage paid to a king or an elder. The Greek proskyneō, which the Gospels use when people kneel before Jesus, carries both senses, and a gesture alone cannot settle whom the one bowing takes the other to be.[6]

Islam draws the line where the Psalm draws it, at the Maker. "Do not prostrate to the sun and the moon, but prostrate to Allah, Who created them, if it is Him ye wish to serve" (41:37).[2]

The claim that Christians never prostrate does not survive a look at their own rites. At the start of the Good Friday liturgy in the Roman Rite, the priest and the deacon go to the altar in silence and prostrate themselves, or kneel, while the people kneel. In the Catholic rite of ordination, the men to be ordained lie prostrate while the Litany of the Saints is sung.[7]

In the Orthodox Churches the gesture is a mark of Lent. Each time the Prayer of St Ephrem is said on the weekdays of Great Lent, the faithful make full prostrations, forehead to the floor. Alexander Schmemann called them the Lenten rite par excellence, the bodily sign of repentance, humility and adoration.[8]

What separates the traditions is how often the posture comes and where it stands in prayer. In the Muslim ṣalāh it comes twice in every unit of every prayer, five times a day. In the churches it comes on certain days, in certain rites.

The bottom line

The Gospels show Jesus at prayer in the posture of Abraham, of Moses and Aaron and of the congregation in the Psalms: face to the ground before the God who made him. The posture was at home in biblical religion long before it was a pillar of the Muslim prayer, and the churches have kept it in their most solemn rites.

Christian theology reads the prayer of Gethsemane through the doctrine that Jesus was fully man as well as fully God. The scene itself shows one who asks, weeps and submits to a will greater than his own. That is the servant the Quran describes in the cradle: "I am indeed a servant of Allah: He hath given me revelation and made me a prophet" (19:30), who tells his people, "It is Allah Who is my Lord and your Lord; then worship Him" (3:51).[9] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Matthew 26:36 to 46; Mark 14:32 to 42; Luke 22:39 to 46 (World English Bible).
  2. Quran 22:77; 2:131; 41:37, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Angela Kim Harkins, "Ritualizing Jesus' Grief at Gethsemane", Journal for the Study of the New Testament 41.2 (2018), 177 to 203.
  4. Hebrews 5:7 (World English Bible).
  5. Genesis 17:1 to 8; Numbers 16:20 to 22 and 20:1 to 13; Psalm 95:1 to 7 (World English Bible).
  6. On proskyneō as homage and as worship, see for example Matthew 2:11, 18:26 and 28:9 (World English Bible).
  7. The Roman Missal, Friday of the Passion of the Lord, no. 5; United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, "The Roman Missal and the Celebration of the Lord's Passion on Good Friday".
  8. Alexander Schmemann, Great Lent: Journey to Pascha (Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1969), on the Prayer of St Ephrem.
  9. Quran 19:30; 3:51, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
